reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes paying for a StrongBlock node by presenting projected passive rewards of about $100 per day and roughly $40,000 annually, then encourages viewers to enter sooner. The offer requires purchasing 10 StrongBlock tokens for one node and paying ongoing fees, while the video emphasizes the unusually large projected return and potential price growth. Although price volatility and gas fees are mentioned, those caveats do not remove the video's active solicitation of participation in the paid node-income opportunity.

opening.argument: Judge, the dollar figures are conditional projections, not a promise of fixed income. The speaker expressly holds the token price constant for the calculation, calls the daily token amount an estimate, and warns that gas costs can substantially increase the monthly expense. Those qualifications matter when deciding whether this is misleading solicitation or investment commentary that leaves material uncertainty visible.

provided that a price of the coin doesn't change
in actuality the fee of $15 a month to run one node it turns into about a hundred and about 170 at the price of gases right now for one node

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes $100 daily and $40,000 yearly, but its own daily-dollar quote includes the unchanged-price condition. Nor is the purchase cost concealed: the speaker describes entry as expensive. The timing opinion is bullish, but it does not turn a conditional calculation into a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: if you got $100 that you're making every single day from here, provided that a price of the coin doesn't change
It is a pretty expensive venture for those of you who do want to get started with this.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A price condition and fee warning do not change the central pitch: the speaker translates paid node participation into daily income, compares its annual projection to a job, and urges earlier entry. Those are affirmative inducements, even without an unconditional guarantee.

if you do want to try to get into this system the sooner the better

opening.argument: Judge, this is substantially an explanation of how the node arrangement works. The speaker says he will cover what it is and how it works, then clarifies the operational distinction: participants pay someone else to run a node. He also situates StrongBlock within an update on coins he personally stakes. Showing an arrangement and calculating possible returns does not, by itself, establish that he guarantees those returns or operates the service.

citations.quote: i'll go into the details of how it works why it exists and what you can earn from it as well
you're actually paying for somebody else to run a node
We gave you an overview of all the coins that I'm staking. Now I am going to be adding more to this and talking more about the ones that are on here.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the price projection and entry advice as the whole video. Yet the speaker also explains the node's function and explicitly identifies the payment-for-operation model. His stated intention to discuss positives and negatives supports reading the earnings discussion as part of a review, not proof of a guaranteed payout.

citations.quote: you're actually paying for somebody else to run a node
There are a bunch of other positives and negatives that go along with StrongBlock

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Explaining the mechanism does not neutralize the promotion. The speaker tells viewers the paid entry requirement, immediately connects it to daily token rewards, and later urges them to enter sooner. The quoted explanation confirms that payment is central to the proposed income opportunity.

citations.quote: if you do acquire 10 StrongBlock tokens you can run 1 node and then you're gonna be earning as you can see all the nodes right here .1 strongblock token rewards every single day
if you do want to try to get into this system the sooner the better

opening.argument: Judge, the described transaction has an identifiable service component: the speaker says payment supports someone else running a node, and he discloses a recurring node fee. The material also separately invites viewers to a Patreon membership for early videos and a discussion community. These details do not establish a credential-harvesting request, a downline recruitment arrangement, or a guaranteed cash payout. A paid service and a creator membership should be evaluated on what is actually shown, not on an unshown fraud mechanism.

citations.quote: you're actually paying for somebody else to run a node
they do require a fee to be paid about 15 a month
you're getting access to two things that's all of my videos up to two days three days early as well as access to my discord community

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies an upfront token requirement and recurring fees, but those facts alone also fit a paid node service. It does not identify a request to send money to the speaker or show a guaranteed cash payment. The speaker characterizes the arrangement as paying for node operation, which is a narrower claim than a proven fraudulent transfer.

citations.quote: in order to run a node you need to have 10 strong tokens
you're actually paying for somebody else to run a node

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is not limited to credential theft, downlines, or a transfer to the speaker. This pitch explicitly ties buying ten tokens for a node to recurring token rewards, converts those rewards to a roughly $100 daily figure, and recommends entering sooner. Calling node operation a service does not erase that paid-income solicitation.
